AppShell.reason: Its tooltip names a collapsed rail’s glyphs for pointer users only. On a phone the rail is a drawer that never collapses, so every item keeps its visible label.

ChatMessage.reason: Touch has no hover, so its action row always shows, as the spec has it on any screen without hover.

Citation.as: a plain link; no hover preview

ColorInput.as: UIColorWell and the system colour picker

Combobox.as: a text field; suggestions in a sheet on iPhone, anchored on iPad

Command.reason: A keyboard-summoned palette has no phone form. The same commands are found through a search field.

ConfirmDialog.as: a confirmation action sheet, or a sheet with the field of a typed phrase

ConversationPage.reason: On a phone the aside opens in a Drawer from the header, the spec’s own form below 48rem, and the thread keeps the whole width.

DataTable.as: a list on iPhone, a table on iPad

DatePicker.reason: SwiftUI’s DatePicker is the platform’s own, with its own phone form, so the web’s sheet below 30rem does not apply.

DateRangePicker.as: two date fields, one range calendar; a sheet on iPhone, anchored on iPad
DateRangePicker.reason: iOS has no range date picker.

Drawer.as: a sheet from the bottom on iPhone, a side panel on iPad

HoverCard.reason: Touch has no hover, and the preview is never load-bearing. The trigger stays a link, and only the preview is lost.

Markdown.reason: Its citations render as Citation does here: links to the source, without the hover preview.

MasterDetailPage.reason: SplitPane’s split from 48rem of the page’s own width, and below it one pane, as on the web: a NavigationSplitView inside AppShell’s navigation stack does not push its detail on an iPhone.

Menu.as: an action sheet on iPhone, a pull-down on iPad

Menubar.reason: An iPhone has no menubar. On iPad and Mac the system draws the command menus an app declares, so a view never draws one. A screen keeps the same commands in a Menu.

ModeSwitch.reason: Settings owns appearance on iOS, and the Human Interface Guidelines ask an app not to offer its own appearance setting. A native screen follows the system’s mode.

MultiSelect.as: a tag field; checklist in a sheet on iPhone, anchored on iPad

Popover.as: a sheet on iPhone, anchored on iPad

RadarChart.reason: Swift Charts has no radial scale.

Rating.reason: SwiftUI has no rating control, so a set rating is a row of buttons drawing the star and star.fill symbols, and a shown rating is one image with an accessibility label.

RichTextInput.reason: SwiftUI’s text editor edits plain text on iOS 17 and macOS 14, and a native member wraps a platform control. An app edits the text in a Textarea and shows a stored document with RichTextContent.

Select.reason: SwiftUI’s Picker is the platform’s own select, with its own phone form, so the web’s sheet below 30rem does not apply.

SplitButton.reason: The two halves stay buttons, and the menu half opens Menu as it renders here, a sheet of actions on iPhone.

SplitPane.as: iPad side by side; one pane at a time on iPhone

Table.as: a list on iPhone, a table on iPad

ThirdParty.reason: The boundary’s rules are lint rules for web code. A native screen hosts another library’s view through UIViewRepresentable, and declares it as a Bespoke zone.

Toast.as: an in-app banner above the home indicator

Tooltip.reason: Touch has no hover, and a tooltip never carries the only copy of a meaning. A hint that matters goes in visible text.

Tour.as: a sheet per step, pointing at no part of the screen

Tree.as: a DisclosureGroup for each branch, nested by level

Treemap.reason: Swift Charts has no mark that tiles a box by area.

TreeSelect.as: a field row that opens Tree in a sheet, and in a popover on iPad
